subject: science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The word equation for photosynthesis and its reactants and products
The leaf and chloroplast: where photosynthesis happens and how leaves are adapted
How glucose is used by the plant, and the factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis
The word equation for aerobic respiration and why organisms respire
Anaerobic respiration in humans and in microorganisms (fermentation)
The role of photosynthesis and respiration in energy flow through ecosystems

questions.lo: The word equation for photosynthesis and its reactants and products
questions.q: Which word equation correctly shows photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and water (the reactants, on the left) and, using light, makes glucose and oxygen (the products, on the right). The first option is respiration written backwards.

questions.lo: The word equation for photosynthesis and its reactants and products
questions.q: What form of energy does a plant need to carry out photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis needs light energy, which is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts. This is why plants only photosynthesise in the light.

questions.lo: The leaf and chloroplast: where photosynthesis happens and how leaves are adapted
questions.q: In which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs the light needed for photosynthesis. Animal cells have no chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesise.

questions.lo: The leaf and chloroplast: where photosynthesis happens and how leaves are adapted
questions.q: Leaves are usually broad and flat. How does this shape help photosynthesis?
options: It gives a large surface area to absorb light
It stops water from entering the leaf
It keeps carbon dioxide out of the leaf
It makes the leaf heavier so it falls in autumn
questions.explain: A broad, flat leaf has a large surface area, so it can capture as much light as possible. Being thin also lets gases move in and out quickly.

questions.lo: The leaf and chloroplast: where photosynthesis happens and how leaves are adapted
questions.q: What is the name of the tiny holes in a leaf that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out?
questions.explain: Stomata are small holes, mostly on the underside of the leaf, that allow gases to be exchanged with the air. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves through them.

questions.lo: How glucose is used by the plant, and the factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis
questions.q: Photosynthesis makes glucose. What does the plant store excess glucose as?
questions.explain: Glucose is soluble, so plants convert it to insoluble starch for storage in leaves, roots and seeds. Starch can be changed back into glucose when energy is needed.

questions.lo: How glucose is used by the plant, and the factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis
questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the main factors that affects how fast photosynthesis happens?
questions.explain: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature all change the rate of photosynthesis. The colour of the pot has no effect on it.

questions.lo: How glucose is used by the plant, and the factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis
questions.q: A gardener keeps a greenhouse warm and brightly lit but keeps the doors and vents shut all day. Which factor is most likely to be limiting photosynthesis?
questions.explain: With plenty of light and warmth, the plants use up the carbon dioxide in the sealed greenhouse. With no fresh air coming in, low carbon dioxide holds the rate back.

questions.lo: The word equation for aerobic respiration and why organisms respire
questions.q: Which word equation shows aerobic respiration?
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break glucose down into carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy. The first option is photosynthesis; the others are types of anaerobic respiration.

questions.lo: The word equation for aerobic respiration and why organisms respire
questions.q: Why do all living organisms need to respire?
options: To release energy from glucose for their cells to use
To make glucose from carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Respiration releases the energy stored in glucose so cells can use it for movement, growth, keeping warm and building new molecules. It is not the same as breathing.

questions.lo: The word equation for aerobic respiration and why organisms respire
questions.q: A student says: 'Only animals respire; plants just photosynthesise.' Why is this wrong?
options: Plants respire too, all the time, to release energy from glucose
Plants only respire in bright light
questions.explain: Every living cell respires, including plant cells, and they do so day and night. Plants photosynthesise as well, but only in the light.

questions.lo: Anaerobic respiration in humans and in microorganisms (fermentation)
options: Respiration that uses lots of oxygen
Respiration that only happens in plants
questions.explain: 'Anaerobic' means without oxygen. Anaerobic respiration releases energy from glucose but does not use oxygen, so it releases less energy than aerobic respiration.

questions.lo: Anaerobic respiration in humans and in microorganisms (fermentation)
questions.q: When human muscles respire anaerobically during hard exercise, which substance is produced?
questions.explain: In human muscle, anaerobic respiration turns glucose into lactic acid, which causes muscles to ache and tire. Ethanol is produced by yeast, not by humans.

questions.lo: Anaerobic respiration in humans and in microorganisms (fermentation)
questions.q: Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast. Which products does it make?
questions.explain: Fermentation in yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. The ethanol is used in brewing and the carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise.

questions.lo: Anaerobic respiration in humans and in microorganisms (fermentation)
questions.q: A baker adds yeast to bread dough and the dough rises. Which product of fermentation causes this?
questions.explain: The carbon dioxide gas made by the yeast forms bubbles in the dough, which make it rise. The ethanol mostly evaporates during baking.

questions.lo: The role of photosynthesis and respiration in energy flow through ecosystems
questions.q: In a food chain, where does the energy originally come from?
options: From the Sun, captured by plants in photosynthesis
From the air breathed in by animals
It is created by the top predator
questions.explain: Energy enters an ecosystem when producers (green plants and algae) capture sunlight in photosynthesis. It then passes to consumers when they eat.

questions.lo: The role of photosynthesis and respiration in energy flow through ecosystems
questions.q: Why is less energy available to animals higher up a food chain (for example, a fox compared with a rabbit)?
options: Energy is destroyed at each step
Energy is lost at each step, mostly as heat from respiration
Larger animals do not need any energy
questions.explain: At each link in the chain, a lot of energy is used for movement and released as heat during respiration. So less energy is passed on, which limits how long food chains can be.

questions.lo: The role of photosynthesis and respiration in energy flow through ecosystems
questions.q: Besides food, why is photosynthesis by plants and algae so important for other living things?
options: It removes all carbon dioxide from the air forever
It releases oxygen that other organisms need to respire
It uses up the oxygen that plants make
It produces lactic acid for animals to use
questions.explain: Photosynthesis releases oxygen into the atmosphere, which almost all living things need for aerobic respiration. It also helps maintain the balance of carbon dioxide and oxygen in the air.
